title: A pilot study investigating the benefits of a new form of nutritional supplement called “immuno-nutrition” on muscle mass and strength in people on haemodialysis
official: Effect of immuno-nutrition on markers of sarcopenia and systemic inflammation in a haemodialysis population: a feasibility randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Low muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia) are common problems in people receiving haemodialysis which lead to poor quality of life and a higher risk of death. 
Inflammation, caused by the body’s defence (immune) system being activated in response to infection or injury, is another common factor that causes loss of muscle mass and strength in people on haemodialysis. 
Standard food supplements are not effective at increasing muscle mass and strength in people on haemodialysis. This is because inflammation limits protein from food being converted into muscle. 
“Immuno-nutrition” is a new form of food supplement that provides calories and protein like other standard food supplements but also contains extra nutrients that reduce inflammation. In previous studies, immuno-nutrition has been shown to benefit people with cancer, another patient group with high inflammation. 
Recently, we showed that immuno-nutrition improved muscle strength and decreased inflammation in a small study of 14 people on haemodialysis. 
Therefore, the aim of this research is to test the study methods and procedures and to collect information that will help us design a larger, more detailed study in the future.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and over who are receiving three haemodialysis sessions per week for at least 3 hours, whose blood tests show that their potassium levels are normal, and who are not taking any medication that inhibits their immune system.

What does the study involve?
Participants will be randomly assigned (similar to picking names from a hat) to the intervention group (“immuno-nutrition”) or the usual care group (standard food supplement). Both groups will take one supplement daily for 24 weeks.
The following assessments will be made at the start of the study and after 12, 18 and 24 weeks of taking the supplements:
1. Handgrip strength, a measure of muscle strength.
2. Body levels of fat and muscle using a specialist scale.
3. Physical function (walking speed, ability to stand from a chair, balance)
4. Food intake (3-day food diaries)
5. Quality of life (questionnaire)
6. Blood tests to monitor blood chemistry and inflammation

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The study will involve taking an immuno-nutrition supplement or a standard nutritional supplement (usual care), as well as following usual dietetic advice provided by NHS renal dietitians, all of which are not expected to be associated with any risks. However, if participants experience anything untoward, the research team will record this, and they will be closely monitored until it has resolved. Participants will also be monitored regularly to ensure that they are taking the nutritional supplements.
We do not foresee any disadvantages arising from taking part in this study, other than the time the participants give for the study assessments, which will be arranged to take place when participants attend for their routine haemodialysis treatment.
The information we get from this study will help us design and conduct a larger, more detailed study to test the effect of immuno-nutrition on muscle mass and strength, inflammation, and associated beneficial outcomes. We cannot promise any immediate direct benefit to research participants; however, by taking part in the study assessments, participants will be able to monitor how their bodies respond to the supplements.

Where is the study run from?
This study is being conducted at the Royal Derby Hospital renal dialysis unit and Lichfield dialysis centre, which are part of University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to July 2027

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) as part of the Research for Patient Benefit Programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Daniela Viramontes Hörner, mszdv@nottingham.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged >=18 years (no upper age limit)
2. Dialysis regime of >=3 haemodialysis sessions/week for >=3 hours using biocompatible dialysers
3. Able to give informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Treatment with immunosuppressant drugs
2. Body mass index (BMI) >35 kg/m²
3. Pregnancy, breastfeeding or intending pregnancy
4. Expected survival <6 months (prognosis assessed and determined by an experienced consultant nephrologist)
5. Hospitalisation at time of screening
6. Known intolerance/allergy to either supplement (or isolated ingredients)
7. Pre-dialysis serum potassium >5.3 mmol/l
